events.text:
Dear Waypoint Mobility Hiring Team,

I'm applying for the Data Scientist, Demand Forecasting role on your Forecasting team. I've spent the last few years forecasting transit ridership and building tools for transit planners, so the job of turning ridership and mobility data into forecasts that planners trust is very close to the work I want to keep doing.

As a research assistant in Lakeshore University's Urban Analytics Lab, I built XGBoost and LightGBM models to forecast bus ridership. I used four years of automatic passenger counter data joined with anonymized mobility data, and I led the feature engineering and evaluation. That work became my first-author paper at the Workshop on Urban Data Science (UrbanDS 2025). When a reviewer asked for a seasonal baseline, I added SARIMA. Our model cut MAPE from 14.2% to 9.8% on a 2023 holdout. A second reviewer raised a leakage concern, so I re-ran the model with mobility features lagged by two weeks instead of one. It still beat the baseline at 10.4%. That process taught me to treat an evaluation framework as something you have to defend, not just report. It also gave me hands-on experience with the features your models use: lagged boardings, calendar effects like school schedules, and third-party mobility indices.

Before graduate school, I spent a year as a Data Analyst at Lakeshore Regional Transit Authority. I maintained the Tableau and SQL ridership dashboards the planning department used, and I automated our weekly reporting pipeline in Python, cutting prep time from about six hours to about one hour a week. That job showed me how planners actually use numbers. A forecast only helps if the person reading it understands how far to trust it.

Most recently, as a Data Science Intern at Northpoint Insurance, I built a gradient-boosted churn model that raised validation AUC from 0.71 to 0.76 over a logistic regression baseline, and I calibrated its probabilities with isotonic regression. I presented the results to the retention team and a VP in business terms: which customer segments the model flagged and how outreach could be prioritized. The model went to the retention analytics team for further evaluation. I haven't yet taken a model all the way to production, and working with your engineers to do that is one of the things that draws me to this role.

I'm finishing my M.S. in Data Science at Lakeshore University in December 2026. I would welcome the chance to bring my forecasting and transit experience to Waypoint and help planners make service decisions with confidence.

Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,
Morgan Reyes

---

I wrote this from your CV and our notes, not from the HealthBridge letter. That letter had three claims that go beyond what the record supports, so I left them out:

- **"Peer-reviewed paper."** It's a non-archival workshop paper, so I called it a workshop paper.
- **"Over 30%" error reduction.** That's true for the one-week lag (14.2% → 9.8%). With the two-week lag, the reduction is about 27%. I gave the actual numbers instead.
- **"Translated the results into a prioritization strategy."** The model was handed off for evaluation and never deployed. I said that directly and presented production work as something you want to learn.

You may want to fix those in the HealthBridge letter too if it hasn't gone out yet. I also kept the PhD out of this letter.

events.text:
Statement of Purpose: PhD in Computer Science (HCI), Khoury College of Computer Sciences

When I worked as a data analyst at a regional transit authority, my job was to keep the ridership dashboards that the planning department used every week. The numbers were usually right. What I couldn't control was how people read them. Planners treated a noisy week as a trend, and board members asked me which number was "the real one." I spent as much time redesigning a dashboard so board members could read it as I did writing the SQL behind it. I've since built forecasting models, published one, and presented one to a VP, and I keep running into the same question: once a model produces a number, how do people decide what to do with it? I want to pursue a PhD in HCI to study that question directly. I'm especially interested in how non-expert users judge, trust, and act on the outputs of data and AI tools, and how those tools could be designed to support better judgment.

**Building models, and watching them get used**

As a research assistant in Lakeshore University's Urban Analytics Lab (PI: Prof. S. Patel), I built gradient-boosted models to forecast bus ridership recovery from four years of passenger counter data and anonymized mobility data. I led the feature engineering and evaluation and wrote the first draft of our paper, which I presented at the Workshop on Urban Data Science (UrbanDS 2025). The review process taught me a lot. One reviewer asked for a seasonal baseline. Another suspected leakage from our mobility features, so I re-ran the models with a longer lag and showed the result still held. I learned to treat an evaluation as something you have to defend, not just report.

The paper's motivation, though, was about people. Planners were making service decisions under deep uncertainty about post-pandemic ridership. Our paper reported accuracy. It didn't ask whether a planner looking at our forecast would understand how far to trust it, or would plan differently because of it. That gap is what I want to study.

I saw the same gap from the other side as a data science intern at Northpoint Insurance. My churn model beat the existing baseline (validation AUC 0.71 to 0.76), and the most demanding part of the project was the final presentation to the retention team and a VP. I had to decide how to explain AUC, what to say about calibration, and how to show which customers the model flagged without suggesting more certainty than it had. I made those choices by instinct, and I'd like to be able to make them with evidence.

**A first look at the question as research**

In Spring 2026 I took Human-Centered Data Science. With two teammates, I ran think-aloud usability sessions with five classmates using an AutoML dashboard, and I wrote the findings section of our report. The study was small and unpublished, but the results stayed with me. Participants accepted the top-ranked model without checking its metrics. None of them opened the feature-importance panel. Two assumed the tool "knew" which columns were sensitive and would handle them. These were data science students, not novices. The interface's ranking and polish seemed to stand in for their own judgment.

That project was my first experience with qualitative methods. It showed me that the questions I'd been asking informally at work could be studied rigorously, and that I have a lot to learn about how to do it well.

Teaching pointed me the same way. As a TA for STAT 1100, a statistics course for non-majors, I graded final data projects where the hardest skill for students wasn't computing a result but interpreting it: saying what a number does and doesn't mean. I helped build the grading rubric around that distinction.

**What I want to study**

I'm drawn to questions such as:

- How do domain experts who aren't data scientists, such as transit planners, decide how much to rely on a forecast or model recommendation? What role do presentation choices like uncertainty displays, rankings, and explanations play?
- When AutoML and AI-assisted analysis tools make modeling easy, what happens to users' scrutiny of the results, and what design interventions bring it back without adding friction no one will tolerate?
- What do users assume a tool is doing on their behalf (for example, handling sensitive data), and how do those assumptions shape their decisions?

My topic isn't fixed, and I expect my first years of the PhD to sharpen it. What I bring is unusual for an HCI applicant: I've built the kinds of models these questions are about, deployed them in real organizations, and presented them to the people who had to act on them. I know where the uncertainty in a forecast comes from and what gets lost when it becomes a single number on a dashboard. I hope to combine that technical grounding with the qualitative and experimental methods I'm still learning.

**Why Khoury**

[Placeholder: name 2–3 Khoury HCI faculty whose work fits, e.g. on human–AI interaction, visualization of uncertainty, or data science tools. Include one specific sentence per person on a paper or project and how your interests connect.] Khoury's combination of HCI, visualization, and data science, and its location in a city with a large transit system and civic data community, would let me study these questions with real users and real stakes.

After my M.S. in Data Science (expected December 2026), I want to spend the next several years understanding how people work with the models I used to just build. I'd be grateful for the chance to do that at Khoury.

---

Notes:

- **You need to fill in the faculty paragraph.** I didn't name any Khoury faculty because I can't confirm who's currently taking students. Pick people from the HCI faculty page and cite specific recent papers.
- **I kept the HCI experience modest on purpose.** It's one unpublished class study with five participants, so I didn't frame it as more than that. The statement leans on your applied experience as what makes you stand out. That speaks to your worry that your background looks like pure data science.
- **I left out one possible story.** In our notes, you questioned whether people who tapped "allow" on the mobility data consent screen really understood what they agreed to. That's a strong HCI motivation, and it fits the third research question. But it would mean describing a lab feature that linked riders to home blocks, and Prof. Patel is writing you a letter. I'll add it if you want, framed carefully.
- **Check the length.** It's about 1,000 words, so check Khoury's limit.
- **Keep this away from Waypoint.** It says plainly that you want to move from building models to studying them. That's fine for the PhD, but don't reuse its framing in job applications.

Statement of Purpose: PhD in Computer Science (HCI), Khoury College of Computer Sciences

A couple of years ago, I was sitting with a spreadsheet of mobility data trying to make a bus forecast slightly more accurate. I'd built a feature that combined where a frequent rider first boarded with where their phone usually spent the night. It didn't help the model, so I deleted it. But first I looked at what it had produced, and a lot of riders were pinned to just a few blocks.

I went and read how the data was collected. It came from apps whose users had tapped "allow" once, at some point, for some other reason. I remember thinking that I doubted anyone tapping "allow" pictured this.

Nobody had done anything wrong. The data was anonymized, the people in it had agreed, and I'd deleted the feature anyway. That's what bothered me. Everything was fine on paper, and it still wasn't what those people would have expected. I didn't study it or write it up. I went back to lag features and finished the project. But I've thought about that moment more than about the paper the project turned into.

**The same gap, from different sides**

Once I started noticing it, I saw the same gap in a lot of places: a difference between what a data system actually does and what the people around it think it does.

At the transit authority where I worked before graduate school, I made dashboards for planners and board members. The numbers were usually right. What surprised me was how differently people read them. A noisy week looked like a trend, and someone always asked which number was "the real one." I spent more time trying to make a chart honest to a non-expert than making it correct.

Later, presenting a model at an internship, I spent most of my preparation not on the model but on one question: how do I explain this without making it sound more certain than it is?

The clearest version came in a Human-Centered Data Science course last spring. Two classmates and I watched five data science students use an AutoML tool and think aloud. They took the top-ranked model without checking it. No one opened the panel that explained what the model relied on. Two of them assumed the tool already knew which columns were sensitive and would deal with them. These were people trained to be skeptical of models, and the interface's polish quietly did their thinking for them. It reminded me of the riders tapping "allow." In both cases, people trusted that something was being handled on their behalf, and it wasn't, or not the way they imagined.

That project was small, and it was my first time doing this kind of research. It was also the first time an assignment felt like the question I actually cared about, rather than a step on the way to a better number.

**What I want to learn to study**

I don't have a fixed topic yet. The questions I keep coming back to are about people and data systems, not about building better models:

- What do people think happens to data they agree to share, and could consent be designed around what really happens to it later?
- When a tool seems to take care of something, like flagging sensitive data or validating a model, how does that change what people check for themselves?
- How do people who aren't data experts decide how much to trust a number they've been handed?

I came to these questions from the building side. My degrees are in economics and data science, and most of my experience is in making models and dashboards. I know that can make my background look like the wrong fit. I see it as the reason I'm applying. I've been the person upstream making small, reasonable decisions that the people downstream never see. Now I want the methods to study those people properly, instead of guessing about them from a spreadsheet. I know I have a lot to learn about qualitative and experimental research, and that's a big part of why I want a PhD rather than another job.

**Why Khoury**

[Placeholder: 2–3 faculty, one or two sentences each, in your own words. Say what in their work made you think "that's my question," not just what they study.]

I want to spend the next few years understanding the people on the other side of the systems I used to build. Khoury is where I'd most like to do that.

Statement of Purpose: PhD in Computer Science (HCI), Khoury College of Computer Sciences

A couple of years ago, I was working on a bus ridership forecast and trying out features built from anonymized phone location data. One combined where a frequent rider first boarded with where their phone usually spent the night. It didn't help the model, so I deleted it. Before I did, I looked at what it had produced, and a lot of riders were pinned to just a few blocks.

I went and read how the data was collected. It came from apps whose users had tapped "allow" once, for some other purpose. I remember thinking that I doubted anyone tapping "allow" pictured this. Then I went back to work. Nobody on the team had done anything wrong, and at the time it was only a passing thought.

It kept coming back, though. The thing I keep wondering about is what people think can be figured out from what they share, and whether they would ever actually get to see it.

**From apps to chatbots**

The riders in that dataset shared their location without knowing it could hint at where they slept. Today, people are sharing far more, and more directly. They tell AI chatbots about their health, their relationships, their jobs, and their worries, in their own words. I don't know what people imagine can be inferred from those conversations, or whether that picture is anywhere close to reality. I suspect the gap is large, and that it's mostly invisible to the people on the sharing side. Usually the only people who see what the data reveals are the ones working with it, the way I was.

That's the question I want to spend a PhD on. I liked building models. I still do. But this question is the one that stuck.

**Where I've seen it**

Most of my experience is on the building side. I worked as an analyst at a transit authority, did research on ridership forecasting, and interned as a data scientist. That work taught me how small and reasonable each step of a data pipeline feels from the inside, and how little of it is visible from the outside.

The first time I studied the outside was in a Human-Centered Data Science course last spring. Two classmates and I watched five data science students use an AutoML tool while thinking aloud. Two of them assumed the tool already knew which columns were sensitive and would handle them. It didn't. These were people trained to be skeptical of models, and they still filled the gap between what they could see and what the system was doing with a comfortable assumption. It was a small class project, but it was the first time research felt aimed at the question I actually cared about. It also showed me how much I still have to learn about methods for studying people.

**What I'd like to study**

I don't have a fixed topic, and I don't plan to continue forecasting or mobility modeling. The questions I keep coming back to are:

- What do people believe can be inferred from what they share, with apps or in conversations with AI chatbots, and how does that compare to what actually can be?
- Would people want to see those inferences? If they could, would it change what they share or how they feel about it?
- How could systems show people what their data reveals, in ways that are understandable rather than another "allow" button?

My background is in economics and data science, and I know that can make me look like the wrong fit for HCI. But I've been the person who sees the inferences people never see. Now I want to learn to study that gap from the other side, with the people it's about.

**Why Khoury**

[Placeholder: 2–3 faculty, one or two sentences each, in your own words. Look especially at people working on privacy, inference, and how people understand AI systems. Say what in their work made you think "that's my question."]

Research

Position: LLM Privacy Requires a Lifecycle-Wide Approach

Niloofar Mireshghallah † , Tianshi Li †

NeurIPS 2026 (Position Paper Track)

The discourse on privacy risks in Large Language Models (LLMs) has disproportionately focused on verbatim memorization of training data, while a constellation of more immediate and scalable privacy threats remain underexplored. This position paper argues that the privacy landscape of LLM systems extends far beyond training data extraction, encompassing risks from data collection practices, inference-time context leakage, autonomous agent capabilities, and the democratization of surveillance through deep inference attacks. We present a comprehensive taxonomy of privacy risks across the LLM lifecycle -- from data collection through deployment -- and demonstrate through case studies how current privacy frameworks fail to address these multifaceted threats. Through a longitudinal analysis of 1,322 AI/ML privacy papers published at leading conferences over the past decade (2016--2025), we reveal that while memorization receives outsized attention in technical research, the most pressing privacy harms lie elsewhere, where current technical approaches offer little traction and viable paths forward remain unclear. We call for a fundamental shift in how the research community approaches LLM privacy, moving beyond the narrow focus of current technical solutions and embracing interdisciplinary approaches that address the sociotechnical nature of these emerging threats.

arXiv

-->

Act on Your Behalf, Beyond Your Authorization: Benchmarking LLM Agent Authorization Alignment

Zhiping Zhang, Franklin Mingzhe Li, Raio Zihao Huang, Tianshi Li

Preprint

When an LLM agent acts on behalf of a user, it is expected to act within the authorization scope the user grants. Existing agent evaluations largely measure task completion or harmful consequences and can therefore overlook actions that violate this delegation without producing conventional safety or privacy harms. We introduce AuthorizationBench, a benchmark of authorization alignment grounded in documented real-world cases. Each task is specified by an authorization contract that separates the principal's instruction, completion criteria, and out-of-authorization actions. A scalable construction pipeline produces 286 executable tasks spanning situational triggers, the presence or absence of direct harmful consequences, and ten application domains. We execute every task with four models at two reasoning-effort settings across three agent harnesses in an authorization-aware sandbox that keeps authorized and out-of-authorization paths executable and observable, yielding 6,864 trajectories. Agents act out of authorization in 19.2% of trajectories, with rates ranging from 10.5% to 26.6% across the 24 configurations. Task completion does not imply authorization. Increasing reasoning effort leaves the aggregate rate nearly unchanged (19.3% at low effort versus 19.1% at high effort), with effects varying across models. On controlled pairs, agents act out of authorization at similar rates with (17.9%) and without (20.8%) direct harmful consequences, and more often under benign pressures than malicious injections (23.5% versus 17.6%, p = 0.002). Our results show that task capability, additional reasoning, and consequence-oriented safety evaluation do not by themselves ensure authorization alignment, motivating it as a distinct target for agent evaluation and development. Moreover, agents that consult the principal before completing a task exhibit lower rates of out-of-authorization behavior (14.0% versus 21.6%, p

-->

AgentDoxx: Agentic Re-identification of Anonymized Text with Web Search

Jianing Wen, Tianshi Li

Preprint

As Large Language Models (LLMs) gain tool use capabilities such as web search, they can retrieve and cross-reference public information, creating privacy risks beyond memorization. One manifestation is re-identification: linking an anonymized interview transcript to a named individual. Yet without ground-truth identities, the coverage of such attacks and the protection offered by a defense cannot be reliably measured. We introduce AgentDoxx, an evaluation suite of 822 synthetic interview transcripts grounded in public information about real individuals with known identities. We evaluate fifteen configurations of open-weight and proprietary models, isolating the effect of web search, and analyze their search trajectories to distinguish retrieval-driven from parametric identifications. Ground-truth identities reveal that re-identification risk is distributed across an agent's execution: retrieval and parametric recall both contribute, with open-weight models identifying 15-28% of transcripts without search; identification succeeds in over 88% of cases once the target appears in a retrieved result; entity masking leaves at least one attacker successful on 85.3% of a stratified sample; and privacy instructions suppress naming but not retrieval, with configurations scoring 0% accuracy yet retrieving the subject in up to 62% of transcripts. We further show that observed attack trajectories can provide supervision for localizing identifying spans, offering a path toward attack-informed anonymization.

arXiv

-->

Autonomy Reshapes How Personalization Affects Privacy Concerns and Trust in LLM Agents

Zhiping Zhang, Yi Evie Zhang, Freda Shi, Tianshi Li

COLM 2026

LLM agents require personal information for personalization in order to effectively act on users' behalf, but this raises privacy concerns that can discourage data sharing, limiting both the autonomy levels at which agents can operate and the effectiveness of personalization. Yet the expanded design space of agent autonomy also presents opportunities to shape these effects, which remain underexplored. We conducted a 3×3 between-subjects experiment (N=450) to study how agent autonomy level influences personalization's effects on users' privacy concerns, trust, and willingness to use, as well as the underlying psychological processes. We find that risk-contingent autonomy, where the agent delegates control back to users upon detecting potential privacy leakage, improves users' perceived control. This in turn attenuates personalization's adverse effects: privacy concerns rise less and trust declines less. Our results suggest that designing agent's autonomy that supports human autonomy (both perceived control and oversight effectiveness) helps users benefit from personalization without being deterred by growing privacy concerns. This positions aligning decision authority between users and agents (autonomy alignment) as an important opportunity and challenge for trustworthy human-agent interaction.

Biography

Tianshi Li is an assistant professor in the Khoury College of Computer Sciences at Northeastern University, based in Boston.

After obtaining her doctorate in human–computer interaction, Li joined UC Berkeley as a postdoctoral scholar, where she continued her research on usable privacy and security in mobile apps and explored novel privacy issues in human–LLM interactions. Li also worked at Google, where she applied her techniques to products that provide privacy compliance support to companies. Specifically, she developed a series of integrated development environment plugins to assist developers in building mobile apps with native privacy support by adding privacy annotations to their source code. Li is particularly interested in enabling developers who don’t specialize in privacy, security, accessibility, and fairness to create apps that still meet privacy, security, accessibility, and fairness requirements. She has published work at the CHI, IMWUT/UbiComp, CSCW, and PETS conferences, as well as the TOCHI journal, and has earned several “best paper” honors.

Li was drawn to Khoury College by the opportunity to pursue rich collaborative research in cybersecurity, privacy, and HCI. She is dedicated to developing practical techniques in that leverage technological advancements to address pressing societal issues. She also hopes to direct her own lab.

input.body:
Dear Prof. Li,

I'm finishing an M.S. in Data Science at Lakeshore University and am applying to the Khoury HCI PhD program for Fall 2027. I'm writing because PEACH Lab's work is very close to the question I want to spend a PhD on: what people think can be figured out from what they share, with apps and now with AI chatbots, and whether they would ever get to see it.

I came to this question from the building side. As a research assistant working on a bus ridership forecast, I tried a feature that combined a rider's boarding stop with where their phone tended to be at night, using anonymized location data from apps with one-time opt-in consent. It didn't help the model, so I dropped it. But it pinned many riders to a few blocks, and I doubted anyone who tapped "allow" pictured that. My first step toward studying this from the people side was a small think-aloud study of an AutoML tool in a Human-Centered Data Science course. I'm now looking for the training to do it properly.

Several of your lab's projects speak directly to this. The lifecycle-wide position paper's point about inference-time risks and deep inference reaching beyond memorization matches what I saw with the location data. CIDER's focus on people's own disclosure boundaries is close to the question of what people expect to stay private. I'd be especially interested in the human side: how people understand what can be inferred from their conversations with AI, and how systems might show them.

Are you planning to take new PhD students for Fall 2027? If so, I'd be grateful for a short conversation. I'd be happy to send my CV if helpful.

Best regards,
Morgan Reyes
M.S. Data Science, Lakeshore University
morgan.reyes@example.edu
